title: Rapid triage reference: API failure heuristics and action cards
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, on-call friendly reference for rapid triage of common API degradations we see: request timeouts (upstream or runtime), 429 rate-limits, degraded streaming (partial frames, stalls), and sudden elevation in 5xx/error-rate. The goal is a 3–10 minute decision loop: detect, contain, mitigate, escalate. Keep this doc pinned in the SRE Slack channel and the on-call runbook bundle.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Redwood hosted API endpoints and edge proxies in front of Dedicated/Private pools.
- Assumes access: k8s clusters, routing layer (Envoy/Contour), Redis prefix cache, and observability (Grafana, Tempo, Loki).
- For private deployments, many steps are advisory (customer infra may differ).

Quick detection signals (first 90s):
- Timeouts: spike in p50->p95 latency and increasing 504s in Nginx/edge logs. Graph to watch: api.latency.p95, api.requests.504m, envoy.cluster.health.
- 429s: sudden jump in 429 rate, often correlated with request-rate spike or quota enforcement. Metrics: api.rate_limit.rejections, quota.concurrency.
- Degraded streaming: clients report truncated events or stalled stream; internal: long-lived connections increase, partial-chunk errors in runtime logs (stream.err.chunk).
- Elevated error rates: p50 stable but p90/p99 and overall errors increase; check api.errors.5xx and model-runtime.errors.

Immediate action checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Announce on #sre-oncall with one-liner + page reference. E.g. "Investigating p95 latency spike -> timeouts on /v1/complete, started 15:10 UTC".
2) Run quick health checks:
   - curl -i -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/health 
   - kubectl -n redwood get pods -l app=api-gateway --field-selector=status.phase!=Running -o wide
   - kubectl -n redwood logs deploy/runtime-svc -c inference --tail 200 | grep -i error
3) Open Grafana dashboard and pin the following panels: p95 latency, 5xx rate, 429 rate, streaming connection count, cluster CPU/GPU utilization.
4) If traffic surge suspected, check source by client_id / api_key: query logs for client_id and see request rate. If a single client is dominant, consider throttling/unblocking via API key rule.

Decision cards by symptom (short action recipes):
- TIMEOUTS (runtime-backed, e.g., long-gen):
  * Quick heuristics: If p95 latency rises and runtime GPU utilization is >85% and queue length > threshold -> likely head-of-line on model runner.
  * Mitigations: temporarily route to backup model variant with lower latency (e.g., gpt-small-quantized), enable aggressive batching windows to improve throughput OR enable short-circuit cache for repeated prompts.
  * Commands: 
    - curl -X POST "https://controlplane.internal/route" -d '{"route":"fallback-small","conditions":{"cpu>80":true}}'  (use admin route tool)
    - kubectl -n redwood scale deployment runtime-svc --replicas=6
  * Rollback: revert route within 15–30m if quality loss unacceptable.

- 429s (rate-limit rejections):
  * Quick heuristics: If only a small set of API keys are hit, it's client misbehavior or release test. If many keys -> upstream traffic surge or Redis throttle.
  * Mitigations: increase rate-limit for specific API keys (short window), temporarily relax global quota for high-priority customers, enable short-burst capacity.
  * Commands: 
    - Admin UI: Customers -> Select key -> Increase QPS/burst
    - redis-cli -h redis.primary --latency to check latency; if slow, consider failover to replica.
  * Notes: confirm billing/entitlement before raising limits for paid customers; log decision in incident ticket.

- DEGRADED STREAMING (stalling or truncated events):
  * Quick heuristics: Look at connection churn and partial-chunk errors in runtime. If edge shows long TCP write durations -> suspected backpressure (slow consumer). If runtime emits "kv-cache-miss" floods, streaming may stall waiting for KV loads.
  * Mitigations: fallback to polling mode for affected clients (short-term), increase streaming worker pool, evict large KV entries or throttle background pre-fetch.
  * Commands: 
    - kubectl -n redwood scale deployment streaming-proxy --replicas=4
    - ./admin/failover_streaming_consumer --selector=zone=us-west1 --dry-run=false
  * Customer communication: set status to "degraded streaming" and include workaround (polling every 2s).

- ELEVATED ERROR RATES / 5xx spikes:
  * Quick heuristics: Correlate errors with deploy timestamps. Check rollout/ canary failure. If deployment started ~time-of-spike -> rollback candidate.
  * Mitigations: Roll back last canary, enable fallback route to stable model, or scale up replicas to reduce queue pressure.
  * Commands: 
    - kubectl -n redwood rollout undo deployment api-gateway --to-revision=42
    - curl -X POST https://controlplane.internal/fallback -d '{"to":"stable-v2026.01"}'

Containment vs mitigation guidance:
- Containment (fast): reduce blast radius without changing customer workloads much — e.g., pin traffic away from a failing zone, disable streaming for a small subset, throttle problematic API key.
- Mitigation (next 30–60m): apply capacity changes, route to fallback models, increase quota temporarily, or rollback failing deploys.

Escalation and communication:
- If containment fails within 20–30 minutes or customer-impact > 5% of requests, escalate to on-call SRE L2 + Eng on-call and notify Customer Success for high-tier customers. Use incident template in #incident-alerts.
- Include: timeline, impact %, affected endpoints, temporary mitigations, and next steps.

Post-incident checklist (post-mortem starter):
- Collect: traces (Tempo), logs (Loki), metrics (Grafana), recent deploys and config changes.
- Owner: assign a single postmortem owner within 24h.
- Action items: capacity buffer changes, more robust fallback policies, add synthetic streaming probes, fix flaky health checks.

Short heuristics table (for quick thinking):
- High p95 + GPU saturation -> scale / fallback to faster model.
- High 429 + normal infra metrics -> likely rate-limiter config; inspect quota store (Redis) latency.
- Streaming stalls + high open connections -> slow consumer/backpressure; consider per-connection throttles and client workaround (polling).
- Sudden 5xx after deploy -> rollback and check canary configs.

Notes to self / open questions:
- Should we add an automatic fallback route when p95 > X and GPU > Y for > 3 minutes? Risk: silent quality degradations.
- Consider a per-client burst forgiveness policy for the first 30s after onboarding to avoid onboarding spikes causing 429s.
- We need a dedicated synthetic streaming probe for each region (sample payloads + TTL).

Useful links and commands repository:
- Grafana dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/sre/api-degradations
- Incident template: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRE/Incident+Template
- Admin tools: https://admin.redwood.internal/
- Common kubectl snippets: kubectl -n redwood rollout status deployment runtime-svc; kubectl -n redwood get pods -l tier=runtime -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.containerStatuses[*].restartCount}'

End of doc — keep this lean. If more details needed, expand use-case specific runbooks (model-specific, region-specific) and add them as children in Confluence.
